hints: Notice the difference between the quantity length and its SI unit metre in option A.
Recall a physical quantity has a numerical value and a unit, such as force in $\text{N}$ or spring constant in $\text{N m}^{-1}$.
Ask which term can be calculated from measurements - percentage uncertainty is a $\%$ ratio and quark flavour is a category, while $F/x$ gives a value with units.
walkthrough: Identify what counts as a physical quantity: something that can be measured and expressed as a number multiplied by a unit.
Check metre: it is the unit used to express the quantity length, so it is not itself the quantity.
Check percentage uncertainty: it is found from $(\text{absolute uncertainty}/\text{measured value}) \times 100\%$, so it is a dimensionless ratio, not a physical quantity.
Check quark flavour: it names the type of quark, such as up, down or strange, so it is a classification with no magnitude or unit.
Check spring constant: it is defined by Hooke's law $F = kx$, rearranged to $k = F/x$, giving a value in $\text{N m}^{-1}$ that describes stiffness.
Only spring constant has both a measurable magnitude and a unit, so This is option D.

options.A: Metre is the SI base unit of length, not a physical quantity itself.
options.B: Percentage uncertainty is a ratio expressing precision, not a measurable physical quantity with its own unit.
options.C: Quark flavour is a name label such as up or down, not a quantity with magnitude and unit.
options.D: Spring constant is a measurable quantity defined by $k = F/x$ with unit $\text{N m}^{-1}$.
